19203.heading: Automated Information Collection
19203.content:
Automated information collection acquires data through networked services, sensors, transactions, or other systems with little direct human intervention. It determines which people, events, and environments become available for later analysis.

Legal evaluation should ask what is collected, from whom, under what authority, and with what notice. Collection is a distinct activity even when it is tightly coupled to [[Automated Information Processing]] or an [[Autonomous Physical System]].

19206.heading: Automated Feature Engineering
19206.content:
Automated feature engineering searches for transformations that improve a dataset's usefulness to a learning task. It reduces reliance on manual trial and error by generating, evaluating, and selecting candidate representations under a computational budget.

Automation does not remove design choices. The transformation library, exploration policy, evaluation signal, and stopping rule define which representations the system can discover and what it considers useful.

19209.title: Automated Deployment
19209.heading: Automated Deployment
19209.content:
Automated deployment encodes the repeatable operations that install an artifact into an environment. The pipeline selects the package, applies the environment's configuration, deploys it to the target service, and records the result.

Automation reduces manual variation and makes frequent releases practical. Approval and promotion policy can remain deliberate even when the mechanical deployment steps are automated.

Automated content analysis uses computational procedures to classify or measure documents from their language. A hand-coded sample or coding dictionary can train a system that applies categories across a much larger corpus.

The method extends quantitative content analysis but does not eliminate interpretation. Category definitions, coding decisions, preprocessing, and validation determine what the automated counts actually represent.

19215.title: Automated Decision Accountability
19215.heading: Automated Decision Accountability
19215.content:
Automated decision accountability assigns responsibility for the design, operation, review, and consequences of decisions produced with computational systems. It asks who can explain a result, correct an error, and answer for an unjustified effect.

Responsibility cannot disappear inside a model or supply chain. Organizations must connect the purpose of processing, the quality of evidence, the choice of procedure, and the authority to act on the output.

The source contrasts a full Blender render with an OpenGL snapshot of the 3D Viewport. Both become reliable only after the script controls their required scene state.

19224.heading: Autologous Cell Source
19224.content:
An autologous cell source uses cells taken from the same person who will receive the engineered tissue. Immune recognition is generally more favorable than with cells from an unrelated donor.

The source may still be limited by patient health, harvest size, expansion time, cost, and whether the required cell type can be obtained or differentiated reliably.

19227.title: Autoencoder
19227.heading: Autoencoder
19227.content:
An autoencoder is a neural network trained to reconstruct its input at its output. An encoding hidden layer transforms the input into an internal representation, and a decoding layer uses that representation to rebuild the original values.

The architecture must avoid a trivial copy path if its representation is to be informative. Kelleher gives a narrower hidden layer as one bottleneck: the network has to retain useful structure while discarding some redundant information. [[Layer-Wise Autoencoder Pretraining]] once used successive encoders to initialize deep networks, though the book notes that most deep networks no longer require that particular procedure.

As a feature learner, the encoder maps observations into a latent representation while the decoder supplies a reconstruction objective. Sparse, denoising, stacked, and variational variants constrain that representation in different ways.

19230.title: Autocorrelation Feature
19230.heading: Autocorrelation Feature
19230.content:
An autocorrelation feature measures the association between a time series and lagged versions of itself. Values at selected lags reveal repetition, persistence, and characteristic temporal scales.

A collection of lag correlations can distinguish dynamics even when two series have similar marginal distributions. Interpretation must account for trend and nonstationarity, which can create high correlations without a stable repeating mechanism.

Running configure adapts paths and capabilities to the host rather than hard-coding one machine. Dependency options allow users to point the build at platform-specific Boost include and library locations.

19236.title: Auto-Scaling
19236.heading: Auto-Scaling
19236.content: Auto-scaling changes capacity automatically in response to a schedule or measured condition. The book's App Service example adds instances when average CPU use crosses an upper threshold and removes them below a lower threshold, within minimum and maximum limits. Hysteresis and bounds prevent constant oscillation, while the chosen signal must reflect the real bottleneck; adding web instances will not fix a saturated shared database.

19239.title: Authorization
19239.heading: Authorization
19239.content:
Authorization determines whether an identified client is permitted to access a resource or perform an operation. It follows [[Authentication]] because a policy needs a known user, role, or claim on which to base its decision.

Angular route guards can control client navigation, but server-side authorization must protect the corresponding API action. A hidden view is not a secure boundary when a caller can issue its own request.

The stock-checker assigns different read and update capabilities to authenticated users through roles and protected operations. This demonstrates that successful login is not sufficient authority for every feature exposed by an application.

For cloud resources, authorization applies after identity and authentication have been established. It can grant rights according to a user's role and should restrict both human users and automated applications to the operations their work requires.

The cybersecurity model distinguishes authorization from authentication: proving who a user is does not prove that the user may reach every resource. Access-control policy can base authorization on administrator mandates, owner discretion, roles, or contextual rules.

The design-patterns source extends the inventory web application so logged-in users are not automatically permitted to perform every product action. Restricted pages and operations require a role or policy check on the server; the cloud discussion makes the same distinction when an external identity provider supplies a token but the application retains its own access rules.
links: TLS Authentication and Secure Remote Access

19242.title: Authorization Policy
19242.heading: Authorization Policy
19242.content:
An authorization policy is a named set of requirements that an authenticated request must satisfy before protected ASP.NET Core code runs. A controller or action can reference the policy declaratively instead of repeating access checks in its body.

Policies keep permission logic separate from HTTP coordination and can be reused across endpoints. Authentication establishes the principal evaluated by the policy; it does not by itself guarantee authorization.

19245.sourceSearchName: authoring by performance authoring by performance
19245.title: Authoring by Performance
19245.heading: Authoring by Performance
19245.content:
Authoring by performance records a person carrying out an intended spatial action and converts that demonstration into reusable AR content or behavior. Motion, timing, speech, pointing, and interaction with physical objects can all supply authoring input.

The approach lets creators express situated behavior in the environment where it will occur. The system must decide which details belong to the reusable specification and which were incidental to the recorded performance.

19246.title: Authoring by Performance
19246.heading: References

19248.title: Authored Story
19248.heading: Authored Story
19248.content:
An authored story is a deliberately shaped narrative carried by a game. Its creator arranges plot, characters, context, rules, images, words, animation, and sound to communicate particular events or ideas.

Authorship can range from a fixed story shown alongside play to a story expressed through the playable system itself. It does not exclude player action, but the available material and paths are intentionally provided by the creator.

19250.title: Authentication

19251.title: Authentication
19251.heading: Authentication
19251.content:
Authentication is the process of verifying that a person or automated system is the identity it claims to be. A web application commonly collects credentials or completes a trusted-provider exchange before establishing an authenticated user.

Authentication answers who the client is; [[Authorization]] answers what that identity may view or change. Sessions, tokens, signatures, and second factors are different mechanisms for carrying or strengthening the result.

The stock-checker project separates authentication from permission: a user must first establish an accepted identity before the application considers which stock operations that identity may perform. IdentityServer issues the token used to carry that authenticated relationship to the API.

Within a cloud [[Security Container]], authentication follows identification and establishes whether a claimed person, application, system, or connected device is legitimate. Evidence may be something the claimant knows, something it possesses, or a biometric characteristic.

Authentication is one of the six security goals in the source's [[Cybersecurity Goal Model]]. It can combine knowledge, possession, and biometric evidence; using several categories reduces dependence on any one credential before [[Authorization]] evaluates access.

The inventory web application adds a login boundary before restricted product operations, while the cloud chapter describes delegating identity proof to a provider and accepting its token. In both cases, establishing identity is only the first step; the server still has to enforce permissions for each protected operation.
links: TLS Authentication and Secure Remote Access

19253.title: Authentication Factor Categories
19253.heading: Document

19254.sourceSearchName: authentication factor categories authentication factor categories
19254.title: Authentication Factor Categories
19254.heading: Authentication Factor Categories
19254.content:
Authentication evidence can be grouped into something a claimant knows, something the claimant has, and something the claimant is. Passwords represent knowledge, tokens or registered devices represent possession, and biometrics represent physical characteristics.

Combining independent categories through [[Multi-Factor Authentication]] makes one stolen credential less decisive. Several steps from the same category do not provide the same diversity of evidence as factors based on different relationships to the claimant.

19257.title: Authenticated User
19257.heading: Authenticated User
19257.content:
An authenticated user is the identity established after the server validates the credentials or token attached to a request. ASP.NET Core makes that principal and its claims available to controller code.

For a write operation, the server can derive authorship from this validated identity rather than trusting a user identifier supplied in the request body. That binds persisted ownership to authentication evidence.

19260.title: Auth0
19260.heading: Auth0
19260.content:
Auth0 is the external identity service configured in the book for the ASP.NET Core API and React client. It authenticates the user, issues tokens for the configured application and API, and exposes identity information to the client session.

The API still validates every presented token and applies its own authorization policy. Delegating identity management does not delegate the application's decisions about which protected operation a user may perform.

19263.sourceSearchName: auslander buchsbaum formula auslander buchsbaum formula
19263.title: Auslander-Buchsbaum Formula
19263.heading: Auslander-Buchsbaum Formula
19263.content:
For a finitely generated module M of finite projective dimension over a Noetherian local ring R, the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula is pd_R(M) + depth(M) = depth(R).

The formula balances homological complexity against regular-sequence depth. A module requiring a longer projective resolution must have correspondingly less depth when the ambient ring remains fixed.

19266.title: Auralization
19266.heading: Auralization
19266.content:
Auralization renders the sound field of a source in space to simulate a binaural listening experience. It attempts to recreate how sound travels and reflects through an environment, making it useful for reverberation.

Wave-based methods solve or approximate the sound-wave equation. Ray-based methods follow paths from source to listener but simplify effects associated with wavelength. Ambisonics records a spherical directional sound field, while wave-field synthesis approximates virtual sources by combining many physical loudspeakers.

Auralization is one route to producing [[Spatial Audio]] for an [[Auditory Display]].

19269.title: Augmented Reality
19269.heading: Augmented Reality
19269.content:
Augmented reality is an approach that uses displays, [[3D Tracking]], and other technologies to enhance a user's view of the real environment with synthetic objects or information.

AR design must account for both physical and virtual content. Display limits, changing lighting, inaccurate registration, and occlusion can make virtual information hard to interpret. Interaction should make it clear how real and virtual objects relate, while controls should avoid hiding important parts of the environment.

AR is part of the broader [[Mixed Reality]] continuum and uses a [[3D User Interface]] when tasks occur directly in a three-dimensional spatial context.

An AR system combines real and virtual information, updates interactively in real time, and keeps corresponding information [[Spatial Registration|registered in three dimensions]]. These requirements do not prescribe a visual or head-worn device: spatial audio or haptic augmentation can also connect information to the physical environment. A working system coordinates tracking, registration, visualization, and a model that relates real and virtual entities.

19272.title: Augmented Paper
19272.heading: Augmented Paper
19272.content:
Augmented paper combines a physical paper artifact with registered digital information or controls. Printed content provides a stable, portable surface, while tracking lets an AR system place imagery or interpret marks and pointing relative to the page.

The paper retains familiar handling and high-resolution static information. Digital augmentation can add change, animation, computation, or links, provided the system preserves alignment as the page or viewer moves.

19275.title: Augmented Matrix
19275.heading: Augmented Matrix
19275.content:
An augmented matrix places the [[Coefficient Matrix]] and right-hand-side vector of a [[Linear System]] side by side, written $[A\mid b]$.

[[Elementary Row Operation|Elementary row operations]] on this matrix represent equivalent operations on the equations. Its echelon form reveals consistency, free variables, and the solution.

19278.title: Augmentation Placement
19278.heading: Augmentation Placement
19278.content:
Augmentation placement describes where generated output appears relative to the user and physical environment. Information may be attached to a world location, an object, the user's body, a display surface, or a moving region controlled by the user.

Placement affects meaning as well as visibility. A world-fixed label identifies a place, an object-fixed overlay follows its referent, and a view-fixed control remains available but no longer claims a physical location.

19281.title: Auditory Display
19281.heading: Auditory Display
19281.content:
An auditory display is an [[Output Device]] that presents information through hearing. In a [[3D User Interface]], a major goal is [[Spatial Audio]] that allows a listener to localize the direction and position of a sound.

Audio can indicate off-screen objects, support [[Wayfinding]], provide ambient realism, substitute for missing touch feedback, encode data through [[Sonification]], or deliver annotation and help. It can be presented through headphones or external speakers, each with different tradeoffs involving comfort, isolation, crosstalk, externalization, and support for multiple listeners.

In AR, generated sound can be spatially registered with a physical source or location and mixed with the sounds already present in the environment. This makes auditory augmentation useful when an object lies outside the visual field or when additional graphics would overload the display.

19283.sourceSearchName: audio visual feature fusion audio visual feature fusion
19283.title: Audio-Visual Feature Fusion
19283.heading: Document

19284.sourceSearchName: audio visual feature fusion audio visual feature fusion
19284.title: Audio-Visual Feature Fusion
19284.heading: Audio-Visual Feature Fusion
19284.content:
Audio-visual feature fusion joins measurements from sound and image streams before the combined representation is classified. Temporal alignment ensures that features describe corresponding moments or events.

Early fusion lets the learner model interactions between modalities directly, but incompatible scales and missing channels can distort the joint vector. Dimensionality reduction or modality-specific normalization may be needed before training.

19285.sourceSearchName: audio visual feature fusion audio visual feature fusion
19285.title: Audio-Visual Feature Fusion
19285.heading: References

19287.title: Audio Snapshot
19287.heading: Audio Snapshot
19287.content:
An audio snapshot is an authored set of temporary mix and effect changes applied across one or more [[Audio Bus|buses]]. Activating it can lower music, emphasize dialogue, add reverb, or otherwise reshape the mix for a situation.

Snapshots can fade in and out rather than switching abruptly. Because they modify routing state rather than replacing every sound, existing event instances continue playing through the transition.

19289.sourceSearchName: audience coverage exit criteria audience coverage exit criteria
19289.title: Audience-Coverage Exit Criteria
19289.heading: Document
19289.content:
2026-09-21 00:27

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Design Evaluation and Handoff]]

19290.sourceSearchName: audience coverage exit criteria audience coverage exit criteria
19290.title: Audience-Coverage Exit Criteria
19290.heading: Audience-Coverage Exit Criteria
19290.content:
Audience-coverage exit criteria require successful playtests with target-audience members, people new to the game, and experienced players. The groups expose different risks: relevance, first-use comprehension, and sustained depth.

No single session proves readiness. Coverage means the design has survived repeated observation across these perspectives with no unresolved failure that threatens the core experience.

19291.sourceSearchName: audience coverage exit criteria audience coverage exit criteria
19291.title: Audience-Coverage Exit Criteria
19291.heading: References

19293.title: Audio Bus
19293.heading: Audio Bus
19293.content:
An audio bus groups sound events into a mix category such as music, dialogue, effects, or ambience. Changing a bus affects every routed event, allowing independent volume control, muting, or processing without visiting each instance.

Buses can form a hierarchy so a master bus governs the full mix while child buses retain category control. An [[Audio Snapshot]] can change several bus settings together for a temporary game state.

19296.title: Audio Bank
19296.heading: Audio Bank
19296.content:
An audio bank is a packaged collection of authored sound events, samples, and metadata loaded by an audio middleware system. Banks let the game request logical events without constructing every DSP setting or asset path in code.

The audio system loads required banks during startup or content transitions and unloads them when no longer needed. Event names and bank versions become a contract between the audio-authoring project and the engine.

19299.title: Audio Reverb
19299.heading: Audio Reverb
19299.content:
Audio reverb is a digital signal processing effect that simulates the many delayed reflections produced by an acoustic environment. Its decay, density, and tonal qualities can make the same sound suggest a small room, large hall, or open space.

Games can associate reverb settings with regions and blend them as the listener moves. The effect communicates environmental character without modeling every physical reflection.

19301.title: Attributed Graph

19302.title: Attributed Graph
19302.heading: Attributed Graph
19302.content:
An attributed graph associates properties with its vertices, edges, or both. The topology expresses relationships while attributes carry types, labels, weights, identifiers, or application data used by queries and updates.

Accelerators must fetch and interpret these values as well as traverse adjacency, so property layout and memory access can be as important as the edge representation.

19305.sourceSearchName: attribute weighted nearest neighbor attribute weighted nearest neighbor
19305.title: Attribute-Weighted Nearest Neighbor
19305.heading: Attribute-Weighted Nearest Neighbor
19305.content:
Attribute-weighted nearest neighbor assigns different importance to feature dimensions when computing proximity. Features with greater discriminatory value contribute more strongly to the distance between a test case and stored observations.

Weights may be learned globally or adapted near the test instance. This changes nearest-neighbor classification into a form of metric learning and can suppress noisy dimensions that would otherwise dominate solely because of their scale or number.

19308.title: Attribute-Level Distance Dispatch
19308.heading: Attribute-Level Distance Dispatch
19308.content:
Attribute-level dispatch asks each AttrInfo object to compare the corresponding values from two records. Continuous metadata can return numeric difference, while discrete metadata can return a simple-match penalty through the same virtual interface.

This division keeps distance algorithms open to new attribute types. It also makes schema identity important because the stored variant alone does not contain enough meaning to choose a comparison.

19311.heading: Attribute Weighting for Clustering
19311.content:
Attribute weighting for clustering assigns different influence to features in the proximity or objective function. It is useful when domain knowledge says some differences matter more than others.

Weights directly change neighborhood geometry and cluster boundaries. They should be justified, tested for sensitivity, and reported as part of the model.

19314.title: Attribute Selection for Clustering
19314.heading: Attribute Selection for Clustering
19314.content:
Attribute selection for clustering chooses the features that define similarity among observations. Irrelevant variables can dominate proximity calculations and obscure the structure the study intends to discover.

The selection should follow the application and data types. For categorical data, redundant attributes can violate useful independence assumptions by counting the same distinction repeatedly.

19317.title: Attribute Selection as Domain Choice
19317.heading: Attribute Selection as Domain Choice
19317.content:
Attribute selection decides which facets of an instance a model may use to distinguish cases. It should be guided by the intended question and domain knowledge, then revised through data exploration and evaluation. Irrelevant fields can create accidental associations; redundant fields can complicate interpretation without adding useful information.

The book contrasts customer-churn projects in two countries where a phone-handset attribute was useful in one and useless in the other because companies offered different upgrade incentives. Predictive relevance thus depends on the local business process, not just on the field name or an algorithm's feature score.

19320.title: Attention
19320.heading: Attention
19320.content:
Attention selects some information for further processing while inhibiting other information. It includes orienting to sensory events, detecting signals for focused processing, and maintaining alertness.

Selective attention chooses what to process, focused attention maintains processing despite distraction, and divided attention attempts to process more than one event at once. Moving attention requires disengaging from one location, shifting, and reengaging elsewhere.

Attention is limited. Overload, peripheral vision limits, rapid events, or divided tasks can cause missed changes and errors. An interface can direct attention toward urgent information, but competing cues may also distract from the primary task.

19323.title: Attention Mechanism
19323.heading: Attention Mechanism
19323.content:
An attention mechanism lets a neural model assign different importance to different parts of its input while producing an output. Instead of forcing all information through one fixed summary, it builds a context weighted toward what is currently relevant.

In an [[Encoder-Decoder Network]], attention helps align an output word or symbol with the input positions that support it. The weights are learned with the rest of the network.

Kelleher presents attention-centered transformer models as an alternative to relying on one fixed sentence vector: the model can dynamically focus on selected input parts while generating an output. He also describes BERT's use of an unlabeled-data pretraining stage followed by smaller task-specific supervised tuning. These were developments discussed in the book's 2019 outlook, not a claim about which architecture currently leads every task.

19326.title: Attention Guidance
19326.heading: Attention Guidance
19326.content:
Attention guidance is the use of composition, motion, threat, contrast, sound, and established rules to lead a player toward important information. It lets the design make something noticeable without removing control of the [[Game Camera]].

Guidance is strongest when the cue already matters to play. A familiar indicator of incoming fire can turn the player's view toward both the threat and a nearby event, preserving the relationship between the player's decision and what is seen.

19329.title: Atomic Operations
19329.heading: Atomic Operations
19329.content:
An atomic operation appears indivisible to competing threads: no observer sees it half-complete. .NET's `Interlocked` operations provide atomic increments, exchanges, additions, and compare-and-swap behavior for selected primitive locations.

Atomic primitives avoid a full lock for small state transitions, but they do not automatically protect a larger invariant spanning several values. Correct lock-free design requires the entire algorithm, not just one assignment, to remain valid under every interleaving.

19335.content:
An atomic challenge is the immediate, indivisible obstacle facing a player during play. It is the lowest level in a [[Hierarchy of Challenges]] and is not composed of smaller subchallenges.

Atomic challenges combine into larger tasks such as encounters, sub-missions, and levels. Their sequence and overlap determine the moment-to-moment texture and difficulty of gameplay.

19341.heading: Atanasoff-Berry Computer
19341.content:
The Atanasoff-Berry Computer was an experimental electronic binary machine designed to solve systems of linear equations. Vacuum tubes performed arithmetic while a rotating mechanism governed its fixed sequence of operations.

John Atanasoff and Clifford Berry demonstrated that electronic calculation at high speed was feasible, but the machine was neither completed nor general-purpose. It represents one path from specialized calculation toward electronic computing.

19344.title: Asynchronous Validator
19344.heading: Asynchronous Validator
19344.content:
An asynchronous validator evaluates a form rule whose result is not available immediately. It returns a future result, commonly through an [[Observable]], and leaves the control pending until that result arrives.

A duplicate-name validator can call a server endpoint because uniqueness depends on stored records rather than the current browser model. The request should be controlled to avoid sending a new server check for every unnecessary keystroke.

19347.title: Asynchronous Programming
19347.heading: Asynchronous Programming
19347.content:
Asynchronous programming represents work that completes later without requiring the initiating thread to wait idly. In an ASP.NET Core data path, repository methods return tasks and controller actions await them before producing the response.

Its primary server benefit is efficient concurrency around I/O. CPU-bound work still consumes processing capacity, and converting only the outer method to async does not remove a synchronous block deeper in the call chain.

19350.title: Asynchronous Messaging
19350.heading: Asynchronous Messaging
19350.content:
Asynchronous messaging lets a sender place a message for later processing without waiting for the receiver to finish. A [[Message Queue]] separates the time at which the producer creates work from the time at which a consumer handles it.

The separation improves decoupling and resilience but moves responsibility into delivery rules. Persistence, acknowledgments, ordering, retries, and the consequences of duplicate or delayed work must be defined.

19352.title: Asynchronous Play

19353.title: Asynchronous Play
19353.heading: Asynchronous Play
19353.content:
Asynchronous play lets participants act at different times without requiring simultaneous connection. Players may join, take a turn or perform an activity, and leave while the shared game continues.

This structure reduces scheduling pressure but needs durable state, notifications, deadlines, and rules for inactivity. Challenges should remain meaningful when response may arrive much later.

19356.sourceSearchName: asynchronous order processing asynchronous order processing
19356.title: Asynchronous Order Processing
19356.heading: Asynchronous Order Processing
19356.content:
Asynchronous order processing accepts an order before every downstream business step has completed. A producer records a message, and a background worker later persists the order and emits a confirmation for the next part of the system.

This design absorbs traffic surges because requests accumulate in a queue instead of demanding an immediate worker. It also changes the user experience: acceptance is not the same as final fulfillment, so later rejection and status feedback must be represented honestly.

19359.title: Asynchronous Controller Action
19359.heading: Asynchronous Controller Action
19359.content:
An asynchronous controller action returns a task and awaits asynchronous repository or service operations. While an external operation is incomplete, the request does not need to occupy a thread that can perform no useful work.

This can improve server scalability under concurrent I/O-bound requests, but it does not make the underlying database operation intrinsically faster. The asynchronous path should extend through the dependencies rather than blocking inside them.

19362.title: Asynchronous Assistant
19362.heading: Asynchronous Assistant
19362.content:
An asynchronous assistant can continue a task after the immediate conversational turn and return when a result or event becomes available. The user does not have to hold an open synchronous exchange while external work completes.

The [[Dialog Manager]] must preserve task state, associate a late result with the correct request, and choose an appropriate time and channel for notification. This behavior often overlaps with [[Proactive Assistant|proactive interaction]].

19365.content: Asynchronous command processing accepts a state-changing request and completes its work after the initiating call has moved on. CQRS can use a queue to decouple a command producer from its handler and absorb spikes in write demand. The caller then needs a way to learn whether the command succeeded, and the handler must consider retries, duplicate delivery, and when the read model will reflect the change.

19368.title: Asymmetric Game
19368.heading: Asymmetric Game
19368.content:
An asymmetric game gives players different starting conditions, rules, roles, resources, or victory conditions. Fairness depends on the total opportunities each side receives rather than identical components.

Asymmetry can create distinctive strategies and cooperation, but it is harder to tune. A unique ability becomes unfair when its advantages are not offset by meaningful costs, limitations, or opposing tools.

19371.content:
C# 8 introduced asynchronous streams so a sequence can produce values over time without blocking while each value becomes available. A producer returns `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, and a consumer processes it with `await foreach`.

This model combines the incremental nature of enumeration with asynchronous waiting, making it suitable for paged services, streamed data, and other sources that do not complete all at once. Cancellation and disposal remain important because enumeration may hold resources across multiple awaits.

19374.title: Asymmetric Error Costs
19374.heading: Asymmetric Error Costs
19374.content:
Two kinds of classification mistake can have very different consequences. In the book's medical example, missing an ill patient may be more serious than sending a healthy patient for additional testing. A single proportion-correct score hides that difference.

Evaluation should therefore reflect the task's actual error costs and decision thresholds. The preferred model is not necessarily the one with the highest unweighted accuracy; it is the one whose mistakes and benefits fit the setting in which people will act on its outputs.

19377.title: Asymmetric Collaboration
19377.heading: Asymmetric Collaboration
19377.content:
Asymmetric collaboration gives participants different interfaces, information, mobility, or roles within one shared task. A mobile worker may stream a first-person AR view while a stationary expert uses a desktop or immersive overview to inspect the wider scene.

The differences can complement each role, but they also create unequal context and control. Cross-view cues must connect the expert's annotations or route suggestions to what the mobile participant can perceive and act upon.

19380.title: Asymmetric Encryption
19380.heading: Asymmetric Encryption
19380.content:
Asymmetric encryption uses a mathematically related public and private key pair. Data encrypted for a recipient with the public key can be recovered with the corresponding private key, allowing secure exchange without first sharing one secret key.

It is slower than [[Symmetric Encryption]] and is therefore suited to small values such as session keys or signature operations. Secure protocols combine its key-management advantage with symmetric bulk-data performance.

19383.title: Associative Classification
19383.heading: Associative Classification
19383.content:
Associative classification builds a classifier from mined class association rules. Training first discovers candidate patterns and then selects, orders, or combines a subset capable of assigning labels.

At prediction time, several rules may match the same observation. The classifier can use the highest-priority rule, aggregate confidence, or vote across matches; the conflict policy is therefore part of the learned model rather than an incidental implementation detail.

19386.title: Associative Property
19386.heading: Associative Property
19386.content:
The associative property says that regrouping repeated addition or multiplication does not change the result:

$$a+(b+c)=(a+b)+c,$$

$$a(bc)=(ab)c.$$

It justifies suppressing parentheses when an expression contains only a sequence of additions or only a sequence of multiplications. Associativity does not authorize arbitrary regrouping across different operations, and subtraction or division are not associative in general. The property concerns parentheses; changing order instead uses the [[Commutative Property]].

19389.title: Association Rule
19389.heading: Association Rule
19389.content:
An association rule is an implication from one itemset to another, written as an antecedent leading to a consequent. It summarizes how often the sets occur together in transaction data.

Support measures prevalence and confidence measures conditional co-occurrence. The rule is an observed association and does not by itself show causation.

19391.sourceSearchName: association rule confidence association rule confidence
19391.title: Association Rule Confidence
19391.heading: Document

19392.sourceSearchName: association rule confidence association rule confidence
19392.title: Association Rule Confidence
19392.heading: Association Rule Confidence
19392.content:
Association rule confidence is the support count of the union of antecedent and consequent divided by the support count of the antecedent. It estimates how often the consequent appears when the antecedent appears.

A confidence threshold filters rules generated from frequent itemsets. Confidence should be interpreted alongside prevalence because a common consequent can produce a high value without a distinctive relationship.

19395.sourceSearchName: association rule mining association rule mining
19395.title: Association Rule Mining
19395.heading: Association Rule Mining
19395.content:
Association rule mining searches for combinations of categorized attributes that frequently accompany an outcome. Support records how much of the dataset contains a rule, confidence records how often the outcome occurs with it, and lift compares that association with independence.

In legislative analysis, session-level centrality and homophily values can be categorized and tested for combinations associated with re-election. A discovered rule is an empirical association rather than proof of a causal career strategy.

The book develops the search from transaction databases and itemsets: minimum support identifies frequent combinations, the downward-closure property prunes all supersets of an infrequent candidate, and confidence filters the implications generated from the surviving sets. These measures describe co-occurrence rather than causal influence.

19398.heading: Association Rule Extraction
19398.content:
Association rule extraction turns each frequent itemset into candidate antecedent-consequent splits and retains those meeting the minimum-confidence threshold. Every nonempty proper subset can serve as an antecedent.

Confidence relationships can prune weaker candidates during generation. The final rules should still be interpreted for redundancy, prevalence, and practical meaning.

19401.title: Associated Prime
19401.heading: Associated Prime
19401.content:
A prime ideal p is associated to an R-module M when p is the annihilator of some element of M. Equivalently, M contains a cyclic submodule isomorphic to R/p.

The set Ass(M) identifies primes directly visible through module elements. Over a [[Noetherian Ring]], a nonzero module has an associated prime, and a finitely generated module has only finitely many.

19404.title: Associated Graded Ring
19404.heading: Associated Graded Ring
19404.content:
The associated graded ring of a filtered ring is gr(R) = ⊕Rₙ/Rₙ₊₁. Each graded piece records one layer of the filtration after deeper layers are collapsed.

For the [[I-Adic Filtration]], gr_I(R) = ⊕Iⁿ/Iⁿ⁺¹. This converts local or filtered behavior into homogeneous algebra that can be studied with graded methods.

19407.title: Assistant Personality
19407.heading: Assistant Personality
19407.content:
Assistant personality is the consistent set of linguistic and behavioral choices through which a system presents a social character. Vocabulary, tone, timing, humor, voice, and response style all contribute.

Consistency helps users predict the interaction, but personality should support the assistant's role rather than conceal its limitations. A [[Social Virtual Assistant]] must avoid implying human understanding or feelings it does not have.

19410.title: Assistant Skill
19410.heading: Assistant Skill
19410.content:
An assistant skill is a packaged capability that extends what a broader assistant can understand and do. It usually defines a domain, supported intents, required entities, dialog behavior, and access to a relevant service.

A broad [[Personal Virtual Assistant]] must select the right skill through [[Intent Triggering]]. Once activated, the skill can use a narrower [[Intent Schema]] and task-specific [[Dialog Policy]].

19413.title: Asset Validation
19413.heading: Asset Validation
19413.content:
Asset validation automatically checks game assets before or while they enter a build. Rules can detect naming errors, invalid geometry, and violations of memory, polygon, or platform budgets.

The rule set grows from defects the team actually encounters. Early automated rejection prevents malformed assets from becoming slower integration or runtime failures.

19416.title: Assistant Initiative
19416.heading: Assistant Initiative
19416.content:
Assistant initiative is the degree to which the system controls the direction and timing of an interaction. Asking the next question, suggesting an action, or starting a notification are progressively stronger forms of initiative.

High initiative can reduce user effort in a narrow task, but it can also interrupt or constrain the user. [[Mixed-Initiative Dialog]] distributes control according to what each participant knows and needs.

19419.title: ASP.NET Core
19419.heading: ASP.NET Core
19419.content:
ASP.NET Core is an open-source, modular web framework for building HTTP services. It can run cross-platform on .NET Core and separates hosting, configuration, services, and request handling into parts that an application can assemble for its own needs.

An ASP.NET Core application commonly starts a [[Web Host]], accepts traffic through a [[Web Server]], and processes each [[HTTP Request]] through ordered [[ASP.NET Core Middleware|middleware]] before routing it to an endpoint such as an [[MVC Controller]].

Registration order is significant. A request is offered to middleware in pipeline order, so an earlier component can handle it before later endpoints or the Angular fallback are considered.

19434.content:

19437.title: ASP.NET Core HttpClientFactory
19437.heading: ASP.NET Core HttpClientFactory
19437.content:
`IHttpClientFactory` centralizes the creation and configuration of `HttpClient` instances in ASP.NET Core. It supports named or typed clients and manages underlying handlers so applications can reuse connections without treating one manually configured client as an unstructured global dependency.

Central configuration provides a natural place for base addresses, headers, logging, and resilience policies. Consumers receive a client through dependency injection, which makes their external-service dependency visible and easier to replace during tests.

19443.title: Ascending Chain Condition
19443.heading: Ascending Chain Condition
19443.content:
The ascending chain condition says that every increasing sequence of subobjects eventually stops changing. For ideals, a chain I₁ ⊆ I₂ ⊆ ··· is stationary when some stage equals every later stage.

A ring satisfies this condition on ideals exactly when it is a [[Noetherian Ring]]. A module satisfying it on submodules is called Noetherian, linking chain behavior to finite generation.

ASP.NET Core filters run at defined stages around MVC action execution and result processing. They support cross-cutting behavior such as validation checks, logging, exception policies, and response modification without repeating code in every action.

Filters can be registered globally or applied to selected controllers and actions. Their scope and order should be kept explicit because hidden control flow can make request behavior harder to understand and test.

19449.title: Aseptic Cell Culture
19449.heading: Aseptic Cell Culture
19449.content:
Aseptic cell culture prevents bacteria, fungi, and other contaminants from entering a living-cell experiment. Work is performed in a sterile-air biosafety hood, with gloves, containers, and tools disinfected before they cross into the working area.

Contamination can kill cells or silently alter their behavior, making sterility part of experimental validity rather than mere cleanliness.

19452.title: As-Is and To-Be Analysis
19452.heading: As-Is and To-Be Analysis
19452.content:
As-is and to-be analysis compares how an organization currently delivers services with the future state it intends to reach. The as-is view records existing applications, infrastructure, contracts, processes, risks, and responsibilities; the to-be view describes the desired cloud-enabled arrangement.

The gap between the views becomes migration work. Making both explicit prevents a cloud transition from being treated as a simple technical relocation when it also changes costs, controls, integration, and ownership.

19455.title: Artinian Module
19455.heading: Artinian Module
19455.content:
An Artinian module satisfies the [[Descending Chain Condition]] on submodules. Every decreasing sequence of submodules eventually becomes stationary.

A module has finite [[Module Length]] exactly when it is both Artinian and Noetherian. Over a Noetherian ring, an Artinian module has finitely many associated primes, all of which are maximal.
